lead.t: Meningoencephalitis is also associated with acute infection with measles, rubella, respiratory viruses (adenovirus, coronaviruses, influenza virus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus), rotavirus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, or rabies.\n

b: Entry via bite wound — infected saliva contacts mucosa or broken skin
Virus replicates locally at bite site in muscle cells
Binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and enters peripheral nerve endings
Travels via retrograde axonal transport to CNS — spinal cord then brain
Causes encephalitis — predominant involvement of limbic system , hippocampus, and brainstem

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rabies is a fatal encephalitis transmitted by infected animal saliva. Early wound care and post‑exposure prophylaxis can prevent disease, but once symptoms appear mortality approaches 100%.

sections.p: Rabies is a viral encephalitis caused by a negative‑sense RNA rhabdovirus. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion after a bite and laboratory confirmation by detection of viral antigen, RNA, or antibodies.
b: Clinical: prodrome (fever, paresthesia at bite) → furious or paralytic phase
Lab: direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) on skin biopsy, RT‑PCR on saliva, serum/CSF antibodies

t.b: Does the patient have rabies antigen in peripheral nerves? Positive confirms infection; negative does not rule out early disease.
Is viral RNA present? Positive early in symptomatic phase; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and exposure history.
Has the patient seroconverted? Positive after day 7 of symptoms; a negative early test does not exclude disease.

sections.p: Rabies progresses through three stages: prodrome, furious (or paralytic) phase, and coma. Staging guides urgency of post‑exposure prophylaxis and supportive care.
b: Prodrome (≤5 days): nonspecific symptoms, bite site paresthesia
Furious phase: agitation, hydrophobia, hypersalivation
Paralytic phase: flaccid weakness, respiratory failure

sections.p: Transmission occurs when saliva from a rabid animal contacts broken skin or mucous membranes. Dogs account for most human cases worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Dog bite (most common in endemic regions)
Bat bite (important in Americas)
Other mammals (cats, raccoons, foxes)

sections.p: After an incubation of weeks to months, patients develop fever, headache, and paresthesia at the bite site, followed by either a furious or paralytic encephalitic picture.
b: Furious: anxiety, agitation, hydrophobia, aerophobia, hyper-salivation
Paralytic: descending flaccid paralysis, often beginning in the limb of the bite

sections.p: Laboratory confirmation is essential but may be unavailable in low‑resource hospitals; clinical criteria and exposure history become paramount.
b: If DFA or PCR unavailable, collect saliva, serum, and skin biopsy for referral.

t.b: Is there pleocytosis? Mild lymphocytic increase is typical; normal CSF does not rule out rabies.

sections.p: Once neurological signs appear, rapid progression to respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, and death is expected.
b: Hydrophobia or aerophobia
Sudden respiratory collapse
Severe autonomic instability

sections.p: Immediate wound cleansing, passive immunization with HRIG, and active immunization with rabies vaccine are the cornerstone. Supportive ICU care is required for symptomatic patients.
b: HRIG infiltrated around wound neutralizes virus locally; avoids systemic immune complexes.
Inactivated rabies vaccine (cell‑culture) stimulates protective antibodies; given on days 0, 3, 7, 14.
Avoid steroids or antivirals without evidence; they do not improve outcome.

sections.p: Observe vaccinated contacts for 10 days; educate communities on animal vaccination and safe wound care.
b: Complete vaccine series even if bite appears minor.
Report animal for observation; if unavailable, assume rabid.

sections.p: Other causes of acute encephalitis can mimic rabies, especially in tropical settings.
b: Herpes simplex encephalitis – focal temporal lobe signs, CSF PCR positive for HSV.
Japanese encephalitis – mosquito‑borne, often with fever and seizures.
Botulism – descending paralysis without encephalitic signs.

sections.p: Early laboratory tests may be falsely negative, leading to delayed treatment.
b: Negative DFA within 48 h of symptom onset does not exclude rabies.
Serum antibodies may appear only after day 7 of symptoms.

whenToSeekHelp: Any animal bite with unknown vaccination status
Development of hydrophobia, aerophobia, or unexplained neurological signs after a bite

faq.q: Can rabies be treated after symptoms start?
faq.a: No proven therapy exists; once clinical disease appears, mortality is near 100%.

faq.q: Why is HRIG given around the wound?
faq.a: It provides immediate neutralizing antibodies at the entry site before the virus reaches nerves.

faq.q: Is a dog bite always dangerous?
faq.a: In endemic areas, any dog bite should be considered potentially rabid until the animal is observed or vaccinated.
